query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The density of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr can be reduced without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures by substituting a portion of the heavier elements with lighter elements, such as replacing some of the Ta with Ti or adding Al, while maintaining the high-entropy alloy concept.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3
generation.intervention: Substitution of heavier elements with lighter elements, such as replacing some of the Ta with Ti or adding Al
generation.conditions: Maintaining the high-entropy alloy concept, with at least five principal elements in near-equiatomic ratios
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a solid solution with a body-centered cubic (BCC) or face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure
generation.mechanism: The substitution of heavier elements with lighter elements reduces the overall density of the alloy while maintaining its mechanical properties due to the high entropy effect, which leads to the formation of a stable solid solution
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced density without sacrificing mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to 1000 °C; loading conditions: tensile and compressive loading
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of substitution required to achieve the desired density reduction without sacrificing mechanical properties is uncertain and requires further experimentation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys with varying amounts of substitution, measure their density and mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures, and compare the results to the baseline as-cast HfMoTaTiZr
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the density of the substituted alloys is not reduced without sacrificing their mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Among the various systems of alloying elements studied, the Ta 20 Nb 20 Hf 20 Zr 20 Ti 20 alloy seems to be attractive due to its reduced density of 9.94 g/cm 3 [ [2] , [3] ], few publications [ [4] , [5] , [6] ] deal with thr thermodynamic properties of certain compositions of the Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
